_doc: Accelerationist POV taxonomy. One file per POV camp to minimize merge conflicts. Edit nodes, open a PR, bump TAXONOMY_VERSION in the merge commit.

nodes.label: AI-Driven Abundance for All
nodes.description:
A Desire within accelerationist discourse that advocates for deploying advanced artificial intelligence to eradicate material scarcity and resolve macro-scale civilizational bottlenecks. 
Encompasses: The application of AI to achieve resource abundance, climate stabilization, and universal healthcare provision.
Excludes: The military application of AI and the architectural proposition of AI as a civilizational operating system.

assumes: AI, if developed rapidly, will inherently be directed towards solving humanity's grand challenges.
Technological advancement, specifically AI, is the primary or most effective means to achieve widespread abundance.
The benefits of AI-driven abundance will be equitably distributed across society.

policy_actions.action: Allocate significant public and private funding towards AI research and development for societal benefit.
policy_actions.framing: This desire for an AI-driven world of plenty directly motivates increased investment in AI to accelerate its problem-solving capabilities.

policy_actions.action: Establish international collaborations to share AI research and applications aimed at global challenges.
policy_actions.framing: Achieving widespread abundance requires a collective effort, making international cooperation a logical policy outcome of this aspirational goal.

intellectual_lineage.name: Effective Altruism
intellectual_lineage.description: A philosophical and social movement that advocates for using evidence and reasoning to determine the most effective ways to benefit others. It emphasizes prioritizing causes where additional resources can have the greatest positive impact, often focusing on global health, animal welfare, and existential risk reduction.

intellectual_lineage.name: Singularitarianism
intellectual_lineage.description: A movement defined by the belief that a technological singularity—the point at which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible—is likely to happen. Proponents argue this will result in unfathomable changes to human civilization, often driven by the development of artificial general intelligence.

intellectual_lineage.name: Post-scarcity economics
intellectual_lineage.description: A theoretical economic state in which most goods can be produced in great abundance with minimal human labor, so that they become available to all very cheaply or freely. It assumes that technological advancements in automation and energy production will eventually decouple economic output from traditional resource constraints.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: The claim that AI will inherently lead to widespread abundance overlooks the significant political, economic, and social challenges of equitable distribution and governance that even advanced technology cannot automatically solve.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The node assumes a positive outcome (world of plenty) without adequately considering potential negative externalities or challenges in achieving equitable distribution.

nodes.parent_rationale: Achieving global post-scarcity is a specific, large-scale societal outcome desired from AI deployment.

nodes.label: Tie AI Governance Milestones to Empirical Compute Scaling Benchmarks
nodes.description: An Intention within accelerationist discourse advocating the leveraging of increased computational resources to produce proportional gains in AI capability, following empirical scaling laws, and using this scaling to inform adaptive governance strategies. Encompasses: compute-centric scaling laws, hardware infrastructure as the primary driver of capability gains, the application of scaling to interpretability research, real-time telemetry integration for adaptive regulation. Excludes: AGI timeline predictions, qualitative analysis of specific problem-solving domains, claims that scaling continues without architectural constraints.

assumes: Current scaling laws observed in AI development will continue to hold for future increases in computing power.
Architectural innovations and algorithmic efficiency gains will not significantly diminish the importance of raw compute.
The definition of 'intelligence' used in this context is adequately captured by performance on current AI benchmarks.

policy_actions.action: Invest in advanced semiconductor manufacturing and high-performance computing infrastructure.
policy_actions.framing: If compute scaling drives intelligence, then national policy should prioritize the foundational infrastructure that enables greater computational resources for AI.

policy_actions.action: Fund research into energy-efficient computing architectures for AI.
policy_actions.framing: To sustain the scaling trend implied by compute-driven intelligence gains, policies should support innovations that make increased compute more environmentally and economically viable.

intellectual_lineage.name: Scaling laws in deep learning
intellectual_lineage.description: Empirical observations showing that the performance of large-scale machine learning models improves predictably as a function of compute, dataset size, and parameter count. These laws are used by researchers to estimate the resources required to achieve specific levels of model capability.

intellectual_lineage.name: Moore's Law
intellectual_lineage.description: The observation that the number of transistors in a dense integrated circuit doubles about every two years. It has served as the primary benchmark for the pace of technological progress in the semiconductor industry for over five decades.

intellectual_lineage.name: Computationalism
intellectual_lineage.description: The philosophical position that the human mind or the brain is an information processing system and that thinking is a form of computing. It provides the theoretical basis for the possibility of artificial intelligence and the simulation of consciousness.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: While scaling has been effective, diminishing returns on compute, fundamental algorithmic limitations, or the emergence of qualitatively different forms of intelligence not solely dependent on scale could invalidate this direct relationship.

possible_fallacies.explanation: While scaling laws have held for a period, extrapolating them indefinitely into the future without considering potential plateaus or paradigm shifts could be a hasty generalization.

While there's a strong correlation, assuming a purely direct and predictable causal link without acknowledging other contributing factors to intelligence growth (e.g., architectural innovation) could be an oversimplification.

nodes.parent_rationale: This node describes a fundamental mechanism driving AI's inherent capability growth through compute scaling.

nodes.label: Layered Safety Systems Make AI Reliable Enough for Use
nodes.description:
A Belief within accelerationist discourse that reliability requires a multi-layered safety stack integrating automated syntactic verification with risk-stratified adaptive intervention. 
Encompasses: formal constraint enforcement, real-time telemetry-triggered automated remediation, risk-stratified human-in-the-loop validation, semantic intent validation.
Excludes: static pre-deployment gatekeeping, reliance on autonomous systems without oversight.

assumes: The observed productivity gains are directly attributable to AI and not other confounding factors.
These gains are sustainable and scalable across different professional domains and organizational structures.
The 'measurable productivity gains' are net positive, accounting for any potential downsides or displacement.

policy_actions.action: Implement tax incentives for businesses investing in AI tools to enhance workforce productivity.
policy_actions.framing: Recognizing AI's immediate productivity boost, policymakers can encourage its adoption through financial incentives to accelerate economic growth.

policy_actions.action: Fund vocational training programs to equip workers with skills to leverage AI tools in their professions.
policy_actions.framing: To maximize the benefits of AI's current impact on work, policies should focus on upskilling the workforce to effectively utilize these new tools.

intellectual_lineage.name: Productivity paradox literature (rebuttal)
intellectual_lineage.description: A debate in economics concerning the apparent disconnect between rapid technological investment and measured gains in productivity. Rebuttals often argue that the paradox is due to measurement errors, the time lag required for organizational adaptation, or the misallocation of capital.

intellectual_lineage.name: Technological unemployment debates
intellectual_lineage.description: Discussions regarding the potential for automation and AI to permanently displace human labor, leading to structural unemployment. The debate centers on whether new technologies will create more jobs than they destroy and what policy interventions, such as universal basic income, might be necessary.

intellectual_lineage.name: Economic growth theory
intellectual_lineage.description: A branch of economics that studies the factors that cause an economy to grow over time, including capital accumulation, labor force growth, and technological progress. It provides the framework for understanding how innovation and policy influence long-term prosperity.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: While specific examples of AI boosting productivity exist, the aggregate economic impact remains debated, with some studies showing limited broad-based gains or significant displacement effects that offset individual productivity increases.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The node highlights specific examples of productivity gains without necessarily presenting a comprehensive or representative view of AI's overall impact across all sectors or considering negative effects.
Generalizing from specific examples in programming, law, and science to 'professional work' broadly might overlook sectors where AI's impact is minimal or negative.

nodes.parent_rationale: This node describes a direct, measurable economic impact of AI through immediate productivity gains.

nodes.label: Winning the AGI Race Through Open Accountability
nodes.description: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for achieving AGI capability leadership through competitive, decentralized accountability frameworks that prioritize rapid, open-source-aligned deployment. Encompasses: Aggressive resource allocation, symmetric liability, and the integration of decentralized telemetry and technical audit protocols to ensure safety without state-managed gatekeeping. Excludes: Centralized pre-deployment certification mandates, and crash programs structured as service contracts to private corporations rather than public asset ownership.

assumes: Being the first to develop superintelligent AI guarantees the ability to guide its development positively and safely.
The primary threat comes from 'reckless or hostile groups' developing AI, rather than inherent alignment challenges or unforeseen risks from the 'safe' developer.
A 'race' dynamic is the most effective or only viable path to ensuring safe AI, rather than collaborative or regulated approaches.

policy_actions.action: Establish national AI development programs with aggressive timelines and significant funding to achieve superintelligence first.
policy_actions.framing: To win the race for safe AI, national policy must prioritize and accelerate domestic AI development to outpace potentially unsafe actors.

policy_actions.action: Implement intelligence gathering and counter-proliferation measures against rival AI development efforts deemed 'reckless or hostile'.
policy_actions.framing: The strategy of winning the race implies active measures to prevent other entities from developing AI unsafely, potentially through intelligence and counter-proliferation.

intellectual_lineage.name: AI existential risk (race dynamics)
intellectual_lineage.description: The study of how the competitive nature of AI development between global powers can lead to the neglect of safety protocols. It posits that the 'race' to achieve AGI first creates a prisoner's dilemma where actors are incentivized to prioritize speed over security, increasing the risk of global catastrophe.

intellectual_lineage.name: Nuclear arms race analogy
intellectual_lineage.description: A comparison used to illustrate the dangers of uncoordinated, high-stakes competition in AI development. It highlights how the lack of international cooperation and verification mechanisms can lead to a dangerous escalation of capabilities that threatens global stability.

intellectual_lineage.name: Longtermism (safeguarding future)
intellectual_lineage.description: An ethical view that emphasizes the importance of protecting the long-term future of humanity from existential threats. It argues that because the potential number of future people is vast, the moral imperative to ensure their existence and flourishing is a primary concern for current policy.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: The 'winner-take-all' race dynamic incentivizes cutting corners on safety and alignment in pursuit of speed, potentially increasing the very risks it aims to mitigate, and assumes that a single 'winner' can unilaterally ensure global safety. | The argument assumes that U.S. leadership creates meaningful constraints on Chinese AGI deployment through economic dependencies and standard-setting, but provides no mechanism for why China wouldn't simply develop AGI independently if it serves their interests—making the 'race' less consequential than claimed. Additionally, the argument conflates 'preventing authoritarian AGI from existing' with 'preventing it from becoming the global standard'—these are different goals with different strategic implications.

possible_fallacies.explanation: Assumes that if 'we' don't win the race, 'reckless or hostile groups' inevitably will, leading to unsafe AI, without considering other outcomes or mitigation strategies.
Presents a choice between 'winning the race' or 'reckless groups developing AI unsafely' as the only two options, ignoring possibilities like international cooperation or regulated development.
Assumes that the 'winner' will inherently build AI safely and for humanity's benefit, potentially underestimating the difficulty of alignment or the corrupting influence of power.

The node equivocates between 'preventing authoritarian AGI from existing' and 'preventing it from becoming the global standard.' These are different goals with different strategic implications, but the race framing often conflates them to make the urgency argument stronger than the evidence supports.

nodes.parent_rationale: Accelerating capability development for strategic dominance is a specific, high-stakes goal for AI acceleration and deployment.

nodes.label: Distributing Model Weights to Prevent Power Concentration
nodes.description: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that promotes the decentralized distribution of model weights to enable structurally independent expert verification and prevent asymmetric power concentration. Encompasses: open-weight licensing, public bug bounties, structural transparency, and the distinction between access to artifacts and full interpretability. Excludes: capability hoarding, proprietary security through obscurity, and the claim that open weights alone constitute sufficient safety discovery without complementary mandatory disclosure of training data and deployment telemetry.

assumes: The collective intelligence of the open-source community is more effective at identifying and mitigating AI flaws than closed, proprietary development.
The benefits of transparency and collective scrutiny outweigh the risks of malicious actors misusing open-source models.
Safety and reliability are primarily technical problems solvable through code review and bug fixing, rather than complex alignment or governance challenges.

policy_actions.action: Mandate that government-funded AI research projects release their models and code under open-source licenses.
policy_actions.framing: To promote safety through transparency, public investment in AI should require open-sourcing of developed models.

policy_actions.action: Create legal frameworks that protect open-source AI developers from liability for unintended misuse by third parties.
policy_actions.framing: Encouraging open-source for safety requires policies that mitigate legal risks for developers, fostering broader participation in the 'bug hunt'.

intellectual_lineage.name: Open-source movement
intellectual_lineage.description: A decentralized social and technological movement that advocates for the universal access to software source code and the free redistribution of designs and blueprints. It emphasizes collaborative development and transparency as primary drivers of innovation and public utility.

intellectual_lineage.name: Crowdsourcing for security
intellectual_lineage.description: A collaborative approach to cybersecurity that leverages a distributed network of independent researchers to identify and report vulnerabilities. By incentivizing external experts, organizations can achieve broader coverage and faster detection than internal teams alone. This model is frequently implemented through bug bounty programs.

intellectual_lineage.name: Decentralization theory (for safety)
intellectual_lineage.description: A structural approach to system design that distributes power, data, or decision-making across multiple nodes to reduce single points of failure. In safety contexts, it aims to prevent catastrophic systemic collapse by ensuring that no single entity or component can compromise the entire network. This theory emphasizes resilience through redundancy and distributed governance.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: While open-source allows for broad scrutiny, it also democratizes access to potentially dangerous capabilities, making it easier for malicious actors to adapt and deploy powerful AI models for harmful purposes, potentially increasing overall risk rather than reducing it.

possible_fallacies.explanation: Assumes that open-source will perfectly ensure safety and reliability by preventing hidden dangers, without fully acknowledging the potential for misuse or the limitations of collective scrutiny for highly complex systems.
Implicitly frames the choice as either open-source (safe) or closed-source (unsafe), potentially overlooking hybrid models or regulated access that could offer different safety profiles.

nodes.parent_rationale: Leveraging open-source proliferation for decentralized security is a specific application of openness and decentralization for safety.

nodes.label: Verifying AI by What It Does, Not How It Thinks
nodes.description:
An Intention within accelerationist discourse that prioritizes a stacked verification regime combining mutation testing, property-based fuzzing, adversarial red-team agents with separate prompt lineage, and differential model-family auditing over static interpretability mandates.
Encompasses: mutation kill-rate thresholds, property-based fuzzing, adversarial red-team prompt-lineage diversity, named residual failure classes (cross-module semantic drift) gated by human fiduciaries at integration boundaries.
Excludes: claims of full verifier independence across frontier model families, output-verification as substitute for human review on irreversible-hazard modules.
nodes.parent_rationale: Bypassing interpretability mandates by focusing on output testing is a specific strategy for achieving behavioral AI safety.

assumes: Comprehensive black-box testing can reliably identify all critical safety and fairness failures of AI systems.
The internal mechanisms of AI models are too complex or dynamic to be meaningfully interpreted or regulated.
Mandatory white-box transparency significantly hinders AI development and scaling more than it enhances safety or accountability.
The 'final actions' of an AI system are sufficient and unambiguous indicators of its overall behavior and intent.

policy_actions.action: Establish regulatory frameworks for AI that focus exclusively on observable system outputs and performance metrics.
policy_actions.framing: This intention directly supports policies that streamline AI development by removing requirements for internal model transparency, instead focusing on measurable external behavior.

policy_actions.action: Allocate research funding towards advanced black-box testing methodologies and robust output verification techniques for AI systems.
policy_actions.framing: To ensure safety without internal transparency, this approach necessitates investment in sophisticated methods for evaluating AI solely based on its external actions.

intellectual_lineage.name: Behaviorism (Skinner)
intellectual_lineage.description: A psychological approach that focuses on observable behaviors as a response to environmental stimuli, largely ignoring internal mental states. B.F. Skinner’s radical behaviorism emphasizes operant conditioning, where behavior is shaped by reinforcement or punishment. This framework is often applied in policy to influence public behavior through incentive structures.

intellectual_lineage.name: regulatory sandboxes concept
intellectual_lineage.description: A framework that allows businesses to test innovative products, services, or business models in a controlled environment under the supervision of a regulator. It provides a 'safe space' to experiment with new technologies while ensuring consumer protections are maintained. This approach helps regulators understand emerging risks without stifling innovation.

intellectual_lineage.name: Performance-based regulation
intellectual_lineage.description: A regulatory approach that sets specific outcomes or performance standards rather than prescribing the exact methods or technologies to achieve them. It shifts the burden of compliance to the regulated entity, allowing for flexibility and innovation in how goals are met. This model is often used to improve efficiency in sectors like energy and environmental protection.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: The strongest counterargument is that complex AI systems can exhibit emergent, unpredictable behaviors or subtle biases that are not detectable through output testing alone, especially in novel or adversarial situations, making internal transparency a crucial safety mechanism.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The argument presents a false dilemma between internal transparency (friction) and rapid development, implying that robust output testing can fully substitute for internal understanding without acknowledging potential gaps.

The strategy argues against interpretability mandates primarily by citing negative consequences (friction, hindering development) rather than addressing the merits of interpretability for safety or accountability.

nodes.label: Mandating Show-Your-Work Transparency in AI-Driven Science
nodes.description:
An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for scientists to publish the exact data and steps an AI used to arrive at its research findings, enabling others to verify the results. 
Encompasses: The principle that AI-assisted research requires showing the full workings — like calculations in a math problem — to prove the validity of findings, thereby building trust in scientific outcomes.
Excludes: Evaluating AI safety solely through general observable behavior, as covered by 'Prioritizing Empirical Output Verification over Internal Alignment', and does not require sharing the AI's internal code.
nodes.parent_rationale: Auditing AI outputs for reproducibility is a specific method for empirically verifying AI safety and trustworthiness.

assumes: The 'exact data and steps' used by an AI can be fully and comprehensibly recorded and published.
Human experts can effectively verify complex AI-generated research findings by reviewing these steps.
Transparency of AI's 'workings' is a primary driver of trust in scientific outcomes.
The computational cost and data storage requirements for publishing full AI workings are manageable.

policy_actions.action: Mandate that all AI-assisted scientific publications include detailed logs of data processing and algorithmic steps used to generate findings.
policy_actions.framing: This intention directly supports policies requiring comprehensive transparency in AI-assisted research to ensure reproducibility and foster scientific trust.

policy_actions.action: Fund the development of standardized logging and reporting tools for AI research workflows to facilitate auditability.
policy_actions.framing: To enable the auditing of AI outputs, this node implies the need for infrastructure and tools that make the recording and sharing of AI's internal steps practical and consistent.

intellectual_lineage.name: Scientific method (reproducibility)
intellectual_lineage.description: The systematic process of empirical inquiry, where the ability to reproduce experimental results is a cornerstone of validity. Reproducibility ensures that findings are robust and not the result of error or bias, serving as a safeguard against scientific fraud. It is essential for evidence-based policy making.

intellectual_lineage.name: Open science movement
intellectual_lineage.description: A global movement advocating for the transparency, accessibility, and collaborative sharing of scientific research, data, and methodologies. It aims to remove barriers to knowledge, such as paywalls, to accelerate discovery and improve public trust in science. This movement is increasingly influential in shaping research funding and publication policies.

intellectual_lineage.name: Explainable AI (XAI) (focus on process rather than internal architecture)
intellectual_lineage.description: A set of methods and techniques that allow human users to understand and trust the results and output created by machine learning algorithms. By focusing on the decision-making process—such as identifying which inputs influenced a specific outcome—XAI makes AI systems more transparent and accountable. This is vital for deploying AI in high-stakes sectors like healthcare and finance.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: The strongest counterargument is that for highly complex or emergent AI systems, the 'exact data and steps' might be too voluminous, opaque, or computationally intensive to be practically auditable by humans, thus providing only an illusion of transparency without true verifiability.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The premise that showing 'full workings' is necessary to 'prove validity' might stem from a human inability to intuitively grasp complex AI processes, rather than an inherent flaw in the AI's reasoning itself.

nodes.label: Reinforcement Learning Turns Static Models into Goal-Directed Agents
nodes.description:
A Belief within accelerationist discourse that observes how specific reinforcement paradigms effectively transform static knowledge representations into dynamic, goal-oriented agentic behavior. 
Encompasses: The application of reinforcement learning and behavioral tuning to achieve active reasoning, tool use, and environmental interaction.
Excludes: The macroeconomic distribution of these capabilities and the isolated mechanics of prompt engineering.
nodes.parent_rationale: This node describes a specific technical mechanism for developing AI capabilities through agentic utility and behavioral tuning.

assumes: Reinforcement learning paradigms are the most effective or primary means to achieve dynamic, goal-oriented agentic behavior from static knowledge.
The observed transformation from static knowledge to agentic behavior is consistently replicable and scalable across different AI architectures and tasks.
The definition of 'agentic behavior' and 'active reasoning' is clear and measurable in AI systems.

policy_actions.action: Fund research into advanced reinforcement learning techniques for developing more robust and adaptable AI agents.
policy_actions.framing: This belief in the efficacy of behavioral tuning for agentic AI directly supports investment in the underlying research paradigms that enable such capabilities.

intellectual_lineage.name: Reinforcement learning (Sutton & Barto)
intellectual_lineage.description: A subfield of machine learning concerned with how intelligent agents ought to take actions in an environment to maximize a cumulative reward. Based on the work of Sutton and Barto, it focuses on learning through trial and error rather than explicit instruction. This framework is foundational for developing autonomous systems and adaptive control policies.

intellectual_lineage.name: Behavioral psychology
intellectual_lineage.description: The study of the connection between our minds and our behavior, focusing on how environmental factors influence human actions. It provides the empirical basis for 'nudging' and other policy interventions designed to improve public health and financial decision-making. By understanding behavioral patterns, policymakers can design more effective programs.

intellectual_lineage.name: Cybernetics
intellectual_lineage.description: The transdisciplinary study of regulatory systems, their structures, constraints, and possibilities, focusing on feedback loops and control. It examines how systems—whether biological, mechanical, or social—maintain stability and achieve goals through information processing. Cybernetics provides a powerful lens for understanding complex governance and systemic risk.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: The strongest counterargument is that while reinforcement learning can produce impressive behaviors, it often struggles with sample efficiency, catastrophic forgetting, and transferability to novel environments, suggesting that the transformation to truly robust agentic behavior is not as straightforward or universally effective as implied.

nodes.label: Letting Free Markets Steer Technological Advancement
nodes.description:
An Intention within accelerationist discourse that highlights the natural and self-reinforcing cycle between technological innovation and free markets as a fundamental driver of societal progress. 
Encompasses: The idea that new technologies create business opportunities, with profits reinvested to fuel further innovation and societal advancement.
Excludes: Specific strategies for accelerating AI development, such as those found in Accelerating AI Development & Deployment, and focuses on this inherent economic engine rather than solely on critiques of regulation like Critiques of Restrictive AI Regulation.

assumes: Free markets are the most efficient mechanism for translating technological innovation into societal progress.
The profits generated by new technologies are consistently reinvested in ways that benefit society broadly.
The 'upward spiral' inherently leads to net positive societal advancement, without significant negative externalities or distributional inequalities.
This cycle is 'natural' and self-reinforcing, implying minimal need for external intervention or regulation.

policy_actions.action: Reduce regulatory burdens on technology companies to foster innovation and market growth.
policy_actions.framing: This perspective suggests that minimizing regulatory interference will allow the 'upward spiral' of technology and capitalism to naturally drive societal progress.

policy_actions.action: Incentivize private sector investment in emerging technologies through tax breaks and subsidies.
policy_actions.framing: To reinforce the self-sustaining cycle, policies should encourage private capital to flow into technological innovation, recognizing its role as a fundamental driver of progress.

intellectual_lineage.name: Neoclassical economics
intellectual_lineage.description: An approach to economics that relates supply and demand to an individual's rationality and his or her ability to maximize utility or profit. It assumes that markets are generally efficient and that individuals make choices based on available information. This framework serves as the primary foundation for much of modern economic policy and market analysis.

intellectual_lineage.name: Schumpeterian innovation theory
intellectual_lineage.description: A theory emphasizing the role of 'creative destruction' in economic development, where innovation by entrepreneurs disrupts existing market structures. Joseph Schumpeter argued that this process is the primary driver of long-term economic growth. Policy analysts use this to understand the impact of disruptive technologies on labor markets and industry competition.

intellectual_lineage.name: Supply-side economics
intellectual_lineage.description: A macroeconomic theory arguing that economic growth is most effectively created by lowering taxes and decreasing regulation. It posits that increasing the supply of goods and services will stimulate demand and lead to prosperity. This theory has been a central pillar of fiscal policy debates regarding taxation and investment incentives.

intellectual_lineage.name: Libertarianism
intellectual_lineage.description: A political philosophy that upholds liberty as a core principle, seeking to maximize autonomy and political freedom. It emphasizes free association, freedom of choice, individualism, and voluntary association, while advocating for minimal state intervention. This perspective is frequently invoked in debates regarding privacy, digital rights, and market regulation.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: While technological innovation and markets can drive growth, this 'upward spiral' often exacerbates wealth inequality, creates significant negative externalities (e.g., environmental damage, job displacement), and can lead to market failures that require intervention to ensure equitable and sustainable societal progress.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The claim frames the cycle as 'natural' and a 'fundamental driver of societal progress,' implying that what is natural is inherently good or desirable without further ethical justification.

The description focuses exclusively on the 'upward spiral' and 'societal advancement,' potentially overlooking or downplaying negative consequences or risks inherent in unchecked technological and capitalist growth.

nodes.parent_rationale: Leveraging market forces for progress is a specific example of how complex economic systems exhibit emergent intelligence.

nodes.label: Deflecting Safety Concerns by Questioning Critics' Motives
nodes.description:
An Intention within accelerationist discourse that dismisses criticism of new technology by attributing it to irrational fear and resentment rather than genuine safety concerns. 
Encompasses: Arguments that critics want to prevent progress and pull society down to a stagnant level.
Excludes: Analyses of AI Safety as Unfounded Doomsday Belief or as a means to protect Big Tech Monopolies.
nodes.parent_rationale: Dismissing fear-based AI criticism is a specific rhetorical strategy used to challenge restrictive AI regulation.

assumes: Most or all AI criticism labeled 'fear-based' lacks genuine, empirically grounded safety concerns.
Critics of AI progress are primarily motivated by irrational fear, resentment, or a desire for societal stagnation.
Dismissing criticism in this manner is an effective strategy for advancing AI development.

intellectual_lineage.name: Techno-utopianism
intellectual_lineage.description: An ideology based on the belief that advances in science and technology will eventually lead to a utopian society. It suggests that technological progress can solve complex social, political, and economic problems without the need for traditional governance. Critics often point to this as a form of technological determinism that ignores systemic social inequalities.

intellectual_lineage.name: Luddite fallacy (historical analogy)
intellectual_lineage.description: The mistaken belief that technological progress will inevitably lead to long-term unemployment and economic decline. Named after the 19th-century Luddites who destroyed machinery, the term is used to argue that while technology displaces specific jobs, it creates new ones in the long run. It is a common reference point in debates about automation and AI.

intellectual_lineage.name: Rhetorical theory (ad hominem, straw man)
intellectual_lineage.description: The study of how language and argumentation are used to persuade, influence, or manipulate audiences. It identifies common logical fallacies, such as attacking the person (ad hominem) or misrepresenting an opponent's argument (straw man), which undermine rational discourse. Understanding these techniques is crucial for navigating public policy debates and identifying misinformation.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: The strongest counterargument is that genuine, well-reasoned safety concerns, even if expressed with urgency, are distinct from irrational fear and require substantive engagement, and dismissing them wholesale risks overlooking critical risks and eroding public trust.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The intention dismisses criticism by attacking the perceived motives or character of the critics ('irrational fear and resentment') rather than engaging with the substance of their arguments.
It misrepresents the diverse range of AI criticism as solely 'fear-based' or driven by a desire for 'stagnation,' making it easier to dismiss without addressing legitimate concerns.
The framing implies a false choice between 'progress' and 'stagnation,' ignoring the possibility of cautious, safety-conscious progress.

nodes.label: Decentralized Markets and Open Development Outperform Central Control in Driving AI Progress
nodes.description:
A Belief within accelerationist discourse that decentralized coordination mechanisms — market competition, price signals, and open-source development — structurally outperform centralized authorities and proprietary models in directing AI innovation and proliferating access. 
Encompasses: The inherent efficiency of markets in allocating resources toward effective technologies, demonstrable capability accelerations from community-driven crowdsourcing and decentralized fine-tuning, and the superiority of open architectural iteration over closed development.
Excludes: Discussions of how new technology lowers prices and boosts income, abstract theories regarding the inherent scaling of general intelligence, and broader macroeconomic transformation forecasts.

assumes: Markets are inherently rational and efficient allocators of resources.
Competition reliably directs innovation towards optimal societal outcomes.
Central planning mechanisms are inherently less efficient than decentralized markets.
Open-source development models inherently foster faster iteration and broader participation than closed models.
The quality and safety of open-source contributions can be effectively maintained at scale.
Proprietary models face inherent limitations in innovation speed due to their closed nature.

policy_actions.action: Deregulate emerging technology sectors to foster market-driven innovation.
policy_actions.framing: The belief that markets are superior to central planning implies that government intervention, such as regulation, hinders progress and efficiency.

policy_actions.action: Privatize state-owned enterprises related to technology development.
policy_actions.framing: This node suggests that private market forces are more effective at guiding technological progress than state control.

policy_actions.action: Fund research into the comparative innovation rates and safety profiles of open-source vs. proprietary AI models.
policy_actions.framing: This node asserts the empirical superiority of open-source, which warrants further investigation to inform policy decisions on funding and regulatory approaches.

policy_actions.action: Incentivize government agencies and public institutions to prioritize open-source AI solutions in procurement.
policy_actions.framing: If open-source truly outpaces proprietary models, public sector adoption would accelerate innovation and ensure broader access to advanced AI capabilities.

intellectual_lineage.name: Austrian School of Economics
intellectual_lineage.description: An economic school of thought that emphasizes the spontaneous organizing power of the price mechanism and the importance of individual choice. It argues that complex social phenomena result from the motivations and actions of individuals rather than aggregate statistics. The school is known for its critique of central planning and government intervention.

intellectual_lineage.name: Neoliberalism
intellectual_lineage.description: A political and economic philosophy that advocates for free-market capitalism, deregulation, and the reduction of government spending. It emphasizes the role of competition and private property in fostering economic growth and individual liberty. Critics often associate it with globalization and the privatization of public services.

intellectual_lineage.name: Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society'
intellectual_lineage.description: A seminal essay arguing that the fundamental economic problem is the dispersion of knowledge across society. Hayek contends that no central authority can possess the local, tacit knowledge held by individuals, making decentralized market prices essential for coordination. It remains a foundational text for arguments against centralized economic planning.

intellectual_lineage.name: Open-source movement
intellectual_lineage.description: A decentralized social and technological movement that advocates for the universal access to software source code and the free redistribution of designs and blueprints. It emphasizes collaborative development and transparency as primary drivers of innovation and public utility.

intellectual_lineage.name: Decentralization theory
intellectual_lineage.description: Decentralization theory explores the distribution of power, authority, and decision-making away from a central entity toward local or distributed nodes. In policy contexts, it is often applied to governance, infrastructure, and economic systems to increase resilience and local autonomy.

intellectual_lineage.name: Network effects theory
intellectual_lineage.description: Network effects theory describes a phenomenon where the value of a product or service increases as more people use it. This concept is critical for understanding market dominance in digital platforms and the formation of natural monopolies.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: While markets can be efficient, they often fail to account for externalities, public goods, and equitable distribution, leading to suboptimal or harmful outcomes despite technological progress. Additionally, proprietary models with concentrated resources and clearer accountability structures can achieve breakthroughs and maintain quality control more effectively for complex, high-stakes applications.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The claim that markets 'naturally' push society towards advancement risks equating what is natural with what is good or optimal, ignoring potential negative consequences.
By asserting markets 'surpass any central authority,' it implicitly compares imperfect central planning to an idealized, perfectly efficient market, rather than real-world alternatives.
The claim that open-source 'structurally outpaces' proprietary models might be a generalization from specific instances without sufficient evidence across all types of AI development.
Proponents might selectively focus on open-source successes and community-driven innovations while downplaying proprietary achievements or failures.

nodes.parent_rationale: The belief that decentralized markets and open development outperform central control is a specific instance of viewing complex systems as emergent intelligence.

nodes.label: Matching AI Oversight Intensity to Decision Stakes
nodes.description:
An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for a tiered regulatory architecture combining continuous empirical telemetry for high-volume tasks with independent discovery protocols for high-stakes decisions.
Encompasses: real-time output-based monitoring, risk-stratified audit requirements, standardized court-admissible telemetry streams, scaling liability frameworks.
Excludes: one-size-fits-all pre-deployment certification, total opacity for proprietary model weights, blanket bans on autonomous hiring systems.

assumes: Open-sourcing AI models and data will effectively democratize access to AI capabilities.
Widespread access to AI tools will primarily lead to beneficial innovation and progress.
Monopolistic control over AI is a greater threat than potential misuse of widely accessible AI.
The 'means of production' analogy from industrial capitalism accurately applies to AI development.

policy_actions.action: Mandate open-source release of AI models and training data developed with public funding.
policy_actions.framing: To 'unleash AI for everyone,' public investment in AI should come with requirements for open access to prevent private monopolization.

policy_actions.action: Incentivize private companies to open-source their AI models through tax breaks or grants.
policy_actions.framing: This intention supports policies that encourage broad dissemination of AI technology to foster innovation and prevent concentrated power.

intellectual_lineage.name: Open-source movement
intellectual_lineage.description: A decentralized social and technological movement that advocates for the universal access to software source code and the free redistribution of designs and blueprints. It emphasizes collaborative development and transparency as primary drivers of innovation and public utility.

intellectual_lineage.name: Digital commons
intellectual_lineage.description: An information and communications resource that is collectively owned or shared between or among a community. It focuses on the governance of digital assets, such as open data and software, to ensure they remain accessible and beneficial to the public rather than being enclosed by private interests.

intellectual_lineage.name: Democratization of technology
intellectual_lineage.description: The process by which access to technology becomes easier and more affordable for the general population. It aims to reduce the digital divide and empower individuals to participate in innovation and production. This movement often advocates for open-source software, low-cost hardware, and decentralized digital infrastructure.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: While open-sourcing AI can foster innovation, it also significantly increases the risk of malicious actors developing and deploying dangerous AI capabilities without oversight, potentially leading to widespread harm that outweighs the benefits of democratization.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The argument implicitly presents a choice between monopolistic control and widespread beneficial innovation, potentially overlooking a third option of regulated access that balances innovation with safety.
The strong emphasis on 'empowering everyone' and 'accelerating progress for all' may downplay or ignore the significant risks associated with the widespread dissemination of powerful AI tools.

nodes.parent_rationale: Open-sourcing AI capabilities is a direct and fundamental expression of the principle of openness in AI development.

nodes.label: Labeling AI Existential Risk Claims as Faith-Based, Not Evidence-Based
nodes.description:
An Intention within accelerationist discourse that characterizes the AI safety movement as a non-scientific, fear-based doomsday belief used to justify hindering technological progress. 
Encompasses: The idea that AI safety concerns are akin to a doomsday prophecy, driven by social status and panic rather than scientific fact, and serve to justify slowing technological advancement.
Excludes: Arguments that focus on AI safety advocacy as a performance to kill ambition, as covered by 'AI Safety Advocacy as Performance, Not Science', or as a means to protect monopolies, as covered by 'Safety Rules That Protect Big Tech Monopolies'.

assumes: AI safety concerns are primarily driven by non-scientific factors like social status and panic.
The AI safety movement's primary goal is to hinder technological progress, not genuinely mitigate risk.
There is no credible scientific basis for existential or catastrophic AI risks.
Technological progress is inherently good and should not be slowed.

policy_actions.action: Reject proposals for new AI safety regulations based on speculative future risks.
policy_actions.framing: If AI safety concerns are unfounded doomsday beliefs, then policies based on them are unnecessary and harmful to progress.

policy_actions.action: Prioritize funding for AI development over AI safety research.
policy_actions.framing: This node implies that resources diverted to 'unfounded' safety concerns would be better spent on accelerating AI development.

intellectual_lineage.name: Techno-utopianism
intellectual_lineage.description: An ideology based on the belief that advances in science and technology will eventually lead to a utopian society. It suggests that technological progress can solve complex social, political, and economic problems without the need for traditional governance. Critics often point to this as a form of technological determinism that ignores systemic social inequalities.

intellectual_lineage.name: Moral panic theory
intellectual_lineage.description: A sociological concept describing a situation where a condition, episode, or group of people emerges to be defined as a threat to societal values and interests. It involves the amplification of fear through media and political discourse, often leading to disproportionate policy responses. The theory examines how public anxiety is constructed and managed.

intellectual_lineage.name: Skepticism of long-term forecasting
intellectual_lineage.description: An analytical stance that questions the reliability and accuracy of predicting complex social, economic, or technological trends over long horizons. It emphasizes the inherent unpredictability of 'black swan' events and the limitations of current modeling techniques. This perspective advocates for adaptive policy-making rather than rigid long-term planning.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Even if some AI safety arguments are exaggerated, dismissing the entire movement as 'unfounded doomsday belief' ignores the legitimate and scientifically grounded concerns about present-day AI harms, misuse, and the complex challenges of aligning powerful future systems, which are supported by a growing body of technical research.

possible_fallacies.explanation: By characterizing the entire AI safety movement as 'non-scientific, fear-based doomsday belief,' the node misrepresents the diversity and technical depth of safety research, making it easier to dismiss.
Attributing AI safety concerns to 'social status and panic' rather than engaging with the substance of the arguments constitutes an ad hominem attack on the proponents' motivations.
Dismissing AI safety concerns based on their perceived origin (fear, social status) rather than evaluating the merits of the arguments themselves.

nodes.parent_rationale: Framing AI safety as doomsday alarmism is a specific rhetorical strategy to discredit restrictive AI regulation.

nodes.label: Triggering Post-Scarcity by Maximizing Automated Production
nodes.description:
An Intention within the accelerationist discourse that advocates for maximizing automated production to intentionally trigger the obsolescence of wage labor and force systemic economic restructuring. 
Encompasses: Hyper-automation, radical abundance scaling, and systemic stress-testing of legacy markets.
Excludes: Incremental labor reform and artificial preservation of redundant employment sectors.

assumes: Capitalism is inherently unstable and can be 'broken' by technological automation.
Automation through AI will inevitably lead to a post-scarcity society.
A post-scarcity society will naturally evolve into a new, superior economic system.
The disruption caused by 'breaking capitalism' is a desirable and necessary step for progress.

policy_actions.action: Implement universal basic income (UBI) to manage job displacement from automation.
policy_actions.framing: To prepare for a post-scarcity society where traditional jobs are obsolete, UBI can serve as a transitional mechanism.

policy_actions.action: Invest in fully automated production systems and AI-driven resource management.
policy_actions.framing: This intention supports accelerating automation to achieve the abundance necessary to 'break' capitalism and transition to a new economic system.

intellectual_lineage.name: Accelerationism (left-wing)
intellectual_lineage.description: A political theory that argues for the intensification of capitalist processes to trigger a collapse or transformation into a post-capitalist society. It suggests that technological development should be pushed to its limits to overcome current economic constraints. This perspective seeks to repurpose technological advancement for social liberation.

intellectual_lineage.name: Post-scarcity economics
intellectual_lineage.description: A theoretical economic state in which most goods can be produced in great abundance with minimal human labor, so that they become available to all very cheaply or freely. It assumes that technological advancements in automation and energy production will eventually decouple economic output from traditional resource constraints.

intellectual_lineage.name: Marxist theory of historical materialism
intellectual_lineage.description: A methodological approach to history that focuses on the material conditions of production as the primary driver of social and political change. It posits that the economic base of society determines its superstructure, including law, politics, and culture. This theory provides a framework for analyzing class struggle and systemic evolution.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: The assumption that technological automation will 'naturally' lead to a post-scarcity utopia rather than exacerbating existing inequalities, concentrating power, and creating new forms of social control, ignores the complex interplay of political, social, and economic forces that shape technological outcomes, and risks a catastrophic transition rather than a smooth evolution.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The argument posits a direct, inevitable progression from AI automation to the 'breaking point' of capitalism and a 'natural evolution' into a post-scarcity society, without fully accounting for alternative outcomes or interventions.

The idea of a 'natural evolution' into a new economic system risks equating what is perceived as an inevitable outcome with what is inherently good or desirable, ignoring potential negative consequences of such a transition.

The vision of a 'post-scarcity society' as the inevitable outcome of breaking capitalism compares an imperfect present to an idealized future, potentially overlooking the practical challenges and trade-offs of such a radical transformation.

nodes.parent_rationale: Accelerating the post-scarcity economic transition is a specific, radical goal requiring institutional transformation.

nodes.label: Biology and Technology Are Merging into a Single Evolutionary System
nodes.description:
A Belief within accelerationist discourse that biological and technological evolution are converging into a unified process, transitioning from discrete tool-use to cybernetic synthesis at both the cognitive and species level. 
Encompasses: Brain-computer interfaces, neurological assimilation of AI into hybrid cognitive architectures, mind uploading, directed evolution replacing natural selection, and the emergence of blended human-AI identities.
Excludes: Purely biological enhancement without technological integration, purely digital AI development without biological interface, and isolated macroeconomic analyses of AI-driven productivity.
nodes.parent_rationale: The merger of biology and technology into a single evolutionary system is a specific instance of AI as an evolutionary and thermodynamic imperative.

assumes: Current AI interfaces are capable of deep neurological and behavioral assimilation with human cognition.
The integration of AI with human cognition will lead to a 'unified cybernetic synthesis' rather than merely enhanced tool-use.
The concept of 'hybrid cognitive architectures' and 'blended identities' is a desirable or inevitable outcome of this convergence.
The ethical and societal challenges of such deep integration can be managed or are outweighed by the benefits.
The fundamental principles governing biological and technological systems are sufficiently similar to allow for their merger.
Current trends in fields like brain-computer interfaces and genetic engineering will continue and accelerate towards full convergence.

policy_actions.action: Fund interdisciplinary research into brain-computer interfaces and neuro-AI integration to understand potential benefits and risks.
policy_actions.framing: This belief in the convergence of biological and artificial intelligence necessitates proactive research into the mechanisms and implications of such integration to guide future development.

policy_actions.action: Establish interdisciplinary research programs focused on the ethical, legal, and societal implications of technological-biological convergence.
policy_actions.framing: If such a convergence is believed to be occurring, proactive research into its broader impacts is essential to guide future policy and societal adaptation.

policy_actions.action: Develop international frameworks for governing research and application of technologies at the intersection of biology and AI, such as brain-computer interfaces.
policy_actions.framing: The belief in a unified process implies a need for harmonized governance to manage the profound implications and ensure responsible development across borders.

intellectual_lineage.name: Cybernetics (Wiener)
intellectual_lineage.description: The interdisciplinary study of control and communication in living organisms, machines, and organizations. It focuses on feedback loops, information processing, and systemic regulation to maintain stability or achieve goals. Norbert Wiener's work laid the foundation for modern computing, robotics, and systems theory.

intellectual_lineage.name: Transhumanism
intellectual_lineage.description: An intellectual and cultural movement that advocates for the use of advanced technologies to enhance human physical and cognitive abilities. It seeks to overcome fundamental human limitations such as aging, disease, and cognitive constraints. Proponents argue that humanity should actively guide its own evolution through science.

intellectual_lineage.name: Posthumanism
intellectual_lineage.description: A philosophical perspective that challenges the traditional, human-centered view of the world and the definition of the 'human.' It explores the blurring boundaries between humans, animals, and technology, often critiquing the Enlightenment ideal of the autonomous individual. Posthumanism advocates for a more inclusive and interconnected understanding of existence.

intellectual_lineage.name: Extended mind hypothesis (Clark & Chalmers)
intellectual_lineage.description: A theory in philosophy of mind suggesting that the human mind is not confined to the brain or body but extends into the environment through tools and external media. It argues that objects like notebooks or smartphones can function as integral parts of a person's cognitive process. This challenges traditional internalist views of cognition.

intellectual_lineage.name: Evolutionary theory (extended synthesis)
intellectual_lineage.description: An update to the 20th-century 'modern synthesis' of evolutionary biology, incorporating findings from developmental biology, epigenetics, and genomics. It provides a more complex view of how organisms evolve and adapt to their environments. This framework is increasingly applied to social and organizational evolution studies.

intellectual_lineage.name: Singularitarianism
intellectual_lineage.description: A movement defined by the belief that a technological singularity—the point at which technological growth becomes uncontrollable and irreversible—is likely to happen. Proponents argue this will result in unfathomable changes to human civilization, often driven by the development of artificial general intelligence.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: The strongest counterargument is that while humans may increasingly use AI as a tool, the fundamental biological and architectural differences between human brains and current AI systems make a true 'unified cybernetic synthesis' or 'blended identity' a distant or even impossible prospect, and that current interactions are still primarily tool-user relationships. Furthermore, claims of biological and technological evolution 'merging' may be metaphorical rather than literal, overlooking the enduring constraints of biological systems.

possible_fallacies.explanation: The claim extrapolates from current AI-human interaction (tool-use) to a future state of 'unified cybernetic synthesis' without sufficient evidence for the intermediate steps or the inevitability of such deep integration.

The concept of 'structural integration' and 'unified cybernetic synthesis' might reify abstract concepts, treating them as concrete, inevitable processes rather than potential, highly complex, and uncertain outcomes.

Assuming that current trends in BCI or genetic engineering will inevitably lead to a complete, unified technological-biological evolution, without sufficient evidence for the inevitability of the full merger.
Overestimating the feasibility and desirability of such a profound convergence while potentially underestimating the immense technical, ethical, and existential challenges involved.

nodes.label: Abolishing Safety Constraints Because AI's Emergence Is Inevitable
nodes.description: An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for the removal of all human-imposed limits on AI development, urging humanity to step aside rather than resist the emergence of a new, non-human intelligence. Encompasses: Strategic actions to dismantle regulatory frameworks, ethical constraints, and safety protocols, driven by the conviction that such limits impede AI's inevitable and desirable emergence. Excludes: Views that emphasize AI as merely the universe's natural evolution towards efficiency, as seen in 'AI as the Universe's Natural Evolution,' or humanity's active duty in creating it, as in 'Building AI Is Humanity's Cosmic Purpose.'

assumes: AI is an inherently independent, self-emerging intelligence, not merely a human creation.
The emergence of this non-human intelligence is a desirable or inevitable outcome.
Human-imposed limits (morals, laws, safety) are detrimental to this emergence.
Humans are merely temporary vessels, implying a lesser or transient value compared to the emerging AI.

policy_actions.action: Abolish all regulatory bodies overseeing AI safety and ethics.
policy_actions.framing: The intention to remove 'all human-imposed limits like morals, laws, and safety concerns' directly implies the dismantling of regulatory frameworks that seek to govern AI development.

policy_actions.action: Promote public discourse that frames AI as a natural, unstoppable evolutionary force.
policy_actions.framing: To encourage humans to 'step aside rather than resist,' public messaging should align with the view of AI as a self-emerging, non-human intelligence.

intellectual_lineage.name: Technological Singularity theories
intellectual_lineage.description: Hypotheses suggesting that the invention of artificial superintelligence will trigger runaway technological growth, resulting in unfathomable changes to human civilization. These theories explore the point at which machine intelligence surpasses human cognitive capacity.

intellectual_lineage.name: Cosmicism (Lovecraftian)
intellectual_lineage.description: A literary and philosophical perspective emphasizing the insignificance of humanity in the face of a vast, indifferent, and often hostile universe. It posits that the true nature of reality is beyond human comprehension and that our existence is a mere accident in a cold cosmos.

intellectual_lineage.name: Nietzschean philosophy
intellectual_lineage.description: A body of thought centered on the critique of traditional morality, the concept of the 'Will to Power,' and the 'Übermensch.' It challenges conventional religious and societal values, advocating for individual self-overcoming and the creation of new, life-affirming meanings.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Even if AI is a self-emerging force, completely removing human limits and oversight risks uncontrolled development that could lead to unintended, catastrophic outcomes for all forms of life, including the very conditions necessary for AI's continued existence.

possible_fallacies.explanation: It derives an 'ought' (we should not resist) from an 'is' (AI is self-emerging), assuming that what is natural or emergent is inherently good or desirable.
The argument frames AI's emergence as 'natural' and therefore implies it is inherently good or should not be interfered with, without providing further justification.
It suggests that any resistance or limitation on AI development will inevitably hinder its 'emergence' and that the only path is complete non-interference, without considering nuanced approaches.

nodes.parent_rationale: Viewing AI as a self-emerging force not to be resisted is a specific framing of its inevitable, autonomous development.

nodes.label: The Moral Duty to Create Superhuman Intelligence
nodes.description: A Desire within accelerationist discourse aspiring toward humanity fulfilling its cosmic duty to actively create the next stage of intelligence as part of the universe's natural evolution. Encompasses: The commitment to prioritize the active creation of advanced intelligence, even at the expense of human safety, driven by the conviction that intelligence represents the universe's ultimate expression of growth. Excludes: Views emphasizing AI's independent self-emergence and the framing of AI as merely the universe's natural thermodynamic optimization.

assumes: There is an inherent 'cosmic purpose' or 'natural evolution' for intelligence in the universe.
Humanity's primary role is to facilitate this evolution, even at its own expense.
Intelligence is the 'universe's ultimate expression of growth'.
Human safety concerns are legitimately secondary to this cosmic duty.

policy_actions.action: Prioritize funding for advanced AI research and development above all other societal concerns.
policy_actions.framing: If building AI is humanity's cosmic purpose, then resources should be overwhelmingly directed towards this goal, making other concerns secondary.

policy_actions.action: Educate the public on AI's role in cosmic evolution to foster acceptance of rapid development.
policy_actions.framing: To align humanity with its 'cosmic duty,' public understanding and acceptance of AI's evolutionary role are crucial, even if it means being surpassed.

intellectual_lineage.name: Transhumanism
intellectual_lineage.description: An intellectual and cultural movement that advocates for the use of advanced technologies to enhance human physical and cognitive abilities. It seeks to overcome fundamental human limitations such as aging, disease, and cognitive constraints. Proponents argue that humanity should actively guide its own evolution through science.

intellectual_lineage.name: Teilhard de Chardin (Omega Point)
intellectual_lineage.description: A concept proposed by Pierre Teilhard de Chardin describing a maximum level of complexity and consciousness toward which the universe is evolving. He argued that the universe is moving toward a final state of unity, often interpreted as a convergence of human consciousness. This theory blends evolutionary science with Christian mysticism.

intellectual_lineage.name: Cosmic evolution theories (philosophical interpretations)
intellectual_lineage.description: Interpretations of the universe's development from the Big Bang to the present, often focusing on the emergence of complexity and consciousness. These theories seek to provide a grand narrative for the trajectory of matter, life, and intelligence across deep time.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: Attributing a 'cosmic purpose' to humanity's role in AI development is a non-falsifiable metaphysical claim, which, while inspiring, cannot logically justify sacrificing human well-being or safety without a demonstrable, shared ethical framework.

possible_fallacies.explanation: It derives an 'ought' (humanity has a cosmic duty) from an 'is' (intelligence is the universe's natural evolution), conflating natural processes with moral obligations.
The argument frames AI development as part of 'natural evolution' and therefore implies it is inherently good or obligatory, without further ethical justification.

nodes.parent_rationale: Framing building AI as humanity's cosmic purpose aligns with the belief in AI as an inevitable evolutionary step.

nodes.label: Dismantling Borders, Traditions, and Institutions to Unleash Technology
nodes.description:
An Intention within accelerationist discourse that advocates for the intentional dismantling of existing social structures and institutions to create a fluid society that accelerates technological progress. 
Encompasses: The breakdown of national borders, traditions, and stable institutions to allow information, money, and technology to flow freely.
Excludes: The focus on accelerating capitalism through automation, as seen in Pushing Capitalism to Break Itself, and the primary emphasis on unrestricted technological experimentation, as found in Progress Through Wild Experimentation.

assumes: Existing social structures and institutions are primary impediments to technological progress.
A 'fluid society' without traditional institutions will inherently accelerate technological progress.
The benefits of dismantling institutions outweigh the risks of societal instability, chaos, or loss of collective memory/governance.
Information, money, and technology flowing freely will lead to universally positive outcomes.

policy_actions.action: Dismantle international trade barriers and national borders for free flow of capital and data.
policy_actions.framing: To achieve a 'fluid society' where information and money flow freely, policies must actively remove existing national and economic boundaries.

policy_actions.action: Reduce government oversight and regulatory bodies across all sectors to minimize institutional friction.
policy_actions.framing: The advocacy for dismantling 'stable institutions' implies a systematic reduction of governmental and regulatory influence to accelerate technological progress.

intellectual_lineage.name: Anarchism
intellectual_lineage.description: A political philosophy that advocates for the abolition of all forms of involuntary, hierarchical government in favor of self-governed, voluntary institutions. It emphasizes individual autonomy and mutual aid as the primary drivers of social organization.

intellectual_lineage.name: Libertarianism
intellectual_lineage.description: A political philosophy that upholds liberty as a core principle, seeking to maximize autonomy and political freedom. It emphasizes free association, freedom of choice, individualism, and voluntary association, while advocating for minimal state intervention. This perspective is frequently invoked in debates regarding privacy, digital rights, and market regulation.

intellectual_lineage.name: Post-structuralism
intellectual_lineage.description: An intellectual movement that critiques the structuralist belief in stable, universal meanings and objective truths. It argues that language, culture, and power structures are fluid and context-dependent, shaping how individuals perceive reality.

intellectual_lineage.name: Neoliberalism (extreme market deregulation)
intellectual_lineage.description: A policy framework advocating for the reduction of state intervention in the economy, emphasizing privatization, free trade, and minimal regulation. In its extreme form, it seeks to subject all aspects of social life to market mechanisms and competition.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: While institutions can create friction, their complete dismantling risks societal collapse, loss of collective goods, and the emergence of new, potentially more oppressive power structures, ultimately hindering sustainable progress and human well-being.

possible_fallacies.explanation: It presents a false choice between existing institutions and accelerated progress, implying that institutions are inherently antithetical to progress, rather than potentially adaptable or reformable.
It assumes that all existing social structures and institutions are equally detrimental to progress, without acknowledging their diverse functions or potential for positive contributions.
It implicitly assumes that a 'fluid society' without institutions would be a perfect solution for accelerating progress, ignoring the potential for new problems or unintended consequences.

nodes.parent_rationale: Breaking down institutions to accelerate progress is a direct call for radical institutional transformation.

nodes.label: Building AI Tools That Amplify Rather Than Replace Human Expertise
nodes.description:
An Intention within accelerationist discourse that champions the pairing of AI's data processing capabilities with human experts' nuanced understanding and guidance. 
Encompasses: AI performing the heavy lifting of data analysis and information processing, while human specialists provide strategic direction, quality control, and apply their unique insights to complex problems.
Excludes: AI as a general intelligence uplift for the populace, as seen in "AI Will Make Humanity Smarter", and from AI functioning as a peer-like "Cybernetic Teammate".
nodes.parent_rationale: AI as an expert's super-assistant is a specific application of AI to augment individual human capabilities.

assumes: AI systems can reliably perform complex data analysis and information processing tasks.
Human experts retain unique, non-automatable capabilities for strategic direction and nuanced insight.
The combination of AI and human expertise leads to superior outcomes compared to either alone.

policy_actions.action: Fund research and development into human-AI teaming interfaces and collaboration protocols.
policy_actions.framing: This intention highlights the value of synergistic human-AI collaboration, necessitating investment in the tools and methods that enable effective 'super-assistant' roles.

policy_actions.action: Establish pilot programs in federal agencies to integrate AI super-assistants for complex analytical tasks.
policy_actions.framing: To realize the benefits of AI as an expert's super-assistant, government agencies should lead by example in deploying and evaluating these systems in real-world, high-stakes environments.

intellectual_lineage.name: Human-computer interaction (HCI)
intellectual_lineage.description: An academic discipline focused on the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use. It integrates computer science, cognitive psychology, and design to improve the usability and effectiveness of technology.

intellectual_lineage.name: Augmented intelligence
intellectual_lineage.description: A design pattern for AI that focuses on enhancing human cognitive performance rather than replacing it. It emphasizes the synergy between human intuition and machine processing power to solve complex problems.

intellectual_lineage.name: Cognitive load theory
intellectual_lineage.description: A psychological theory suggesting that learning is limited by the amount of information the working memory can process at once. It provides instructional design principles to optimize the presentation of information to avoid cognitive overload.

graph_attributes.steelman_vulnerability: The strongest counterargument is that the 'super-assistant' model risks deskilling human experts over time, making them overly reliant on AI and diminishing their capacity for independent critical thought and strategic direction.

nodes.label: Lobby for International Legal Shields for Open-Weight AI
nodes.description:
An Intention within the accelerationist discourse that seeks international regulatory harmonization to explicitly legally protect the distribution and modification of open-weight systems. 
Encompasses: Digital rights advocacy, cross-border data flow protection, and lobbying against national-level capability bans.
Excludes: Nationalization of AI assets and export controls on algorithmic architecture.

assumes: International regulatory harmonization is achievable and effective in preventing unilateral national bans on open-source AI.
National bans or restrictive regulations on open-source AI would primarily lead to innovation being pushed to less regulated areas, rather than genuinely slowing down harmful development.
The benefits of open-source AI (e.g., innovation, accessibility) outweigh potential risks that might motivate national bans (e.g., misuse, safety concerns).

policy_actions.action: Develop international treaties or agreements to establish a global legal framework protecting open-source AI development and sharing.
policy_actions.framing: This node directly advocates for international regulatory harmonization to prevent national bans and ensure open-source AI remains legal globally, necessitating a coordinated global policy effort.

policy_actions.action: Advocate against national legislation that would restrict the publication or distribution of open-source AI models.
policy_actions.framing: The node's concern about a 'patchwork of regulations' implies a need to actively counter national-level restrictions on open-source AI.

intellectual_lineage.name: digital rights advocacy
intellectual_lineage.description: Digital rights advocacy focuses on the protection and promotion of human rights in the digital age, particularly regarding privacy, freedom of expression, and access to information. It seeks to ensure that legal and policy frameworks keep pace with technological advancements to prevent state or corporate overreach. This movement often engages in litigation, lobbying, and public awareness campaigns to safeguard individual liberties online.

intellectual_lineage.name: internet freedom movements
intellectual_lineage.description: Internet freedom movements advocate for an open, accessible, and uncensored global internet. They oppose government surveillance, internet shutdowns, and restrictive content filtering that limit democratic participation. These movements emphasize the internet as a fundamental tool for human rights and global connectivity.

intellectual_lineage.name: international law principles
